stem: A nurse is comparing resting heart-rate findings for an infant and an older child. Which principle is most accurate when interpreting the values?

options.A: Use one resting heart-rate range for infants and older children because age has little effect on normal values.
options.B: Interpret by age because infants normally have faster resting heart rates than older children and teenagers.
options.C: Expect resting heart rate to rise with age, making higher values more typical in older children than infants.
options.D: Apply adult resting limits after infancy because pediatric resting rates quickly become equivalent to adult values.

rationale: The American Heart Association states that normal resting heart rate varies by pediatric age. Infants have substantially faster average resting rates than older children or teenagers. Therefore B is correct. A ignores age-related variation, C reverses the usual age relationship, and D incorrectly applies adult limits broadly after infancy.
educational_objective: Interpret pediatric resting heart rate using age-specific expectations, recognizing that infants normally have faster resting rates than older children and teenagers.
source_locator: Section ‘Normal ranges for children’ — infant resting heart rate averages 100–190 beats/min; older child or teenager at rest 60–100 beats/min.
source_claim_supported: Normal resting heart rate varies by pediatric age; infants normally have faster average resting rates than older children and teenagers.

options.A: Use one resting heart-rate range for infants and older children because age has little effect on normal values.
options.B: Interpret by age because infants normally have faster resting heart rates than older children and teenagers.
options.C: Expect resting heart rate to rise with age, making higher values more typical in older children than infants.

source_original.rationale: The American Heart Association notes that normal resting heart rate differs by pediatric age: infants average substantially faster rates than older children and teenagers. Option B correctly applies age-dependent interpretation. Option A incorrectly treats pediatric ages as sharing one range. Option C reverses the normal age trend. Option D incorrectly assumes adult limits apply soon after infancy.
source_original.source_detail: American Heart Association — Treating Arrhythmias in Children, Normal ranges for children: infants have faster resting rates (about 100–190) than older children/teenagers (about 60–100). correction_summary: No clinical correction was required. The item was re-anchored to the current live AHA page with an exact section locator and the rationale was tightened to the age-dependent principle actually tested.

audit_findings.source_authority: American Heart Association pediatric arrhythmia guidance.
audit_findings.exact_locator: Normal ranges for children section provides the age-dependent comparison used by the item.
audit_findings.claim_audit: The item tests the direction of the age relationship; the cited numeric examples are directly from AHA and no additional thresholds were introduced.

distractor_audit.A: Incorrect because pediatric resting heart-rate expectations vary with age.
distractor_audit.B: Correct and directly reflects AHA guidance.
distractor_audit.C: Incorrect because it reverses the age relationship.
distractor_audit.D: Incorrect because pediatric rates do not broadly become adult-equivalent immediately after infancy.

audit_findings.ambiguity_second_answer: Only B states the supported age-dependent interpretation.
audit_findings.cueing: Choices are parallel interpretive principles without length or terminology cues.
audit_findings.blueprint: Fits Reduction of Risk Potential through correct interpretation of age-specific monitoring findings.
